entry.title: Business Roles in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, Part 2: The Investigation Toolkit
entry.content:
In Part 1, I covered why a well-designed business role can still leak access: authorizations are cumulative, the least restrictive role wins, and blank is a value. Knowing the rules is half the job. The other half is answering the questions that land in your inbox, with evidence, before someone escalates.

"Who else has this app?" "Which role gives this user access to plant 2000?" "Why can she not find the app we just assigned?" On-premise, you would reach for SUIM and a handful of tables. In Public Cloud, you have a small set of Fiori apps that can answer almost all of these, as long as you know which one to open and which path to take through it.

This part is that toolkit. It also covers one category of app that generates a surprising number of "missing app" tickets: the Standard Navigation Target.

The toolkit: four apps, four kinds of question

Each app answers a different kind of question, and most investigations use two of them together. One looks at the role landscape, one at health indicators, and two at the building blocks SAP delivers.

AppUse it to answerWhat it looks at

IAM Information System

Who has what, and through which role

Your business roles and their relationships: users, catalogs, restrictions, applications, templates and derived roles

IAM Key Figures

Where are the weak spots across the whole system

Health indicators for business roles, with drill-down

Display IAM Apps

What can this app do, and what can it be restricted on

One IAM app: its variants, restriction types and supported access categories

Display Restriction Types

Which apps does a given restriction type control

One restriction type: its fields and where it is used

IAM Information System is the primary reporting tool. It offers six standard views, each built around the business role: Business Role to Business User, to Business Catalog, to Restriction, to Application, to Business Role Template, and to Derived Business Role. If you think in SUIM terms, this is where most of those questions now live.

IAM Key Figures gives you four charts: number of assigned business roles, roles with default values, business roles with unmaintained restrictions, and unrestricted business roles. The last two map directly to the two failure modes from Part 1. One complains loudly, the other stays quiet, and this app shows you both before a user does.

Display IAM Apps and Display Restriction Types describe what SAP delivers, not what you built. Use them in design workshops, before you promise a restriction that the app does not support.

Recipes for the questions that actually arrive

These are the paths I use most. None of them is complicated. The value is in knowing which question goes to which app.

"Which users have this app?"

  1. In Display IAM Apps, filter by the app ID and note every variant. Full, display-only and change-document variants are separate IAM apps.
  2. In IAM Information System, open the Business Role to Application view and filter by those IAM apps. You now have the roles.
  3. Switch to Business Role to Business User for those roles. That is your user list.

Skip step 1 and you will answer for one variant while the auditor is asking about all of them.

"Why can this user see plant 2000?"

  1. In IAM Information System, list every business role assigned to the user.
  2. Open Business Role to Restriction for those roles and look at the restriction type in question.
  3. Look for the role where it sits at Unrestricted, or where 2000 or blank is maintained.

This is the desk version of the build-up method from Part 1. It finds the culprit without a test user, as long as you check every role, not only the one the ticket names.

"Which roles left a restriction unmaintained, or wide open?"

Start in IAM Key Figures, not in the roles. The charts for unmaintained restrictions and unrestricted business roles give you the full list, and the drill-down takes you to the affected roles. Then confirm each one in IAM Information System before you change anything. Some of them will be deliberate, which is exactly why Part 1 recommended writing those decisions down.

"If I restrict on purchasing organization, which apps does it affect?"

Open Display Restriction Types for that restriction type and check where it is used. Then, for each app that matters, confirm in Display IAM Apps which access categories it supports: read, write or value help. This is the check to run before a workshop, not after.

The app that is assigned but cannot be found

Some apps carry the application category Standard Navigation Target (T). They never appear as a tile and cannot be found through search. They open only when the user navigates to them from another app in the same business catalog. SAP documents this in KBA 3633075, using the Supplier app (F0354) as the example.

The ticket usually reads like this: "We added the catalog to the role, the user has the role, and the app is still not there." Everything in the assignment is correct. The authorization model is doing its job. The user is simply looking for an entry point that was never meant to exist.

What I check, in this order:

  1. Confirm the application category in the catalog. If it is Standard Navigation Target, stop treating it as an authorization problem.
  2. Find the app it is reached from. That is usually the one the user actually works in, for example a list or object page with a link to the supplier.
  3. Make sure the user also has that source app, from the same catalog, with restrictions that let them reach the record.

Two design notes follow from this. First, when a requirement says "give the user app X", check the category before you scope the role around it. If X is a navigation target, the real requirement is the app that leads to it. Second, tell your key users early. A one-line note in the role documentation saves the same ticket from coming back after every new hire.

Making it a habit

The toolkit is most useful when you open it before the ticket arrives. A quick look at IAM Key Figures after every role transport, and a Display IAM Apps check before every design workshop, will prevent more incidents than any amount of troubleshooting afterwards.

Part 3 covers the lifecycle: change documents, the Extensibility Inventory, and what actually has to happen around an upgrade.

If you use a path through these apps that I have not covered, or you have hit a navigation target that behaved differently, share it in the comments.

References

  • KBA 3633075 – Standard Navigation Target (T) application category: SAP Knowledge Base
  • KBA 3788562 – Business Roles/IAM Apps/Restriction Types – Frequently Asked Questions
  • Reporting on Business Roles (SAP Learning)
  • IAM Information System (SAP Help Portal)
  • Part 1: Business Roles in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Authorization Model Nobody Explains Before Go-Live

entry.title: Structured Address in Payment Medium Files: A Complete Guide
entry.content:
Introduction

The payments industry is undergoing a significant transformation driven by the adoption of ISO 20022 and increasing regulatory requirements. One important trend is the transition from unstructured postal addresses to structured address information in payment files. To support this transition, SAP has introduced the Structured Address capability for payment medium files.

The feature enables payment files to contain address elements such as street name, house number, building, floor, city, postal code, district, region, and country in dedicated fields rather than free-text address lines. This improves payment processing, bank compliance, sanctions screening, and overall payment quality.

This blog provides an end-to-end overview of the Structured Address feature, including:

  • Business background
  • Solution overview
  • Configuration and verification

Business Background

Traditionally, many payment medium files stored address data in a few free-format address lines:

While this format is human-readable, it is difficult for banks and regulatory systems to interpret consistently.

Structured addresses separate the information into individual attributes. In an ISO 20022 XML payment file this becomes structured tags like <StrtNm>, <BldgNb>, <PstCd>, <TwnNm>, <Ctry>  — each independently addressable by the receiving system.

The structured address solution allows payment medium formats to use dedicated address components for all relevant parties involved in a payment transaction. It improves payment data quality, reduces payment repair and rejection rates, and enables better interpretability between banks ad payment infrastructures. 

Solution Overview

Which Parties are Covered?

The structured address solution supports structured addresses for the major parties that can appear in a payment chain:

Party Type

Description

Structure

Creditor

Party to which an amount of money is due. In a credit transfer, it is usually the supplier receiving the payment.

FPAYHX_CRD

Debtor

Party that owes money to the creditor. In a credit transfer, it is usually the company initiating the payment.

FPAYHX_DBT

Ultimate Creditor

Ultimate party to which an amount of money is due. Typically used when an alternative payee is involved. In this case, the Ultimate Creditor is the supplier to whom the invoice is posted, while the Creditor is the alternative payee receiving the payment.

FPAYHX_UCR

Ultimate Debtor

The party on whose behalf the payment is ultimately made. In a credit transfer, this is commonly used when the sending company code differs from the paying company code. In such cases, the Debtor is the paying company code, and the Ultimate Debtor is the sending company code.

FPAYP_UDB (replaces deprecated FPAYHX_UDR)

Creditor Agent (Beneficiary Bank)

Bank servicing the creditor and receiving the payment on behalf of the creditor.

FPAYHX_CRA

Debtor Agent (House Bank)

Bank servicing the debtor and from which the payment is initiated.

FPAYHX_DBA

Intermediary Agent 1

First intermediary bank in the payment routing chain between debtor and creditor banks.

FPAYHX_AGT1

Intermediary Agent 2

Second intermediary bank in the payment routing chain.

FPAYHX_AGT2

Intermediary Agent 3

Third intermediary bank in the payment routing chain.

FPAYHX_AGT3

One-Time Vendor

A supplier that is not maintained as a regular supplier master record with its own permanent address and bank details. The supplier information is entered for a specific transaction and stored in the accounting document. Structured address data is sourced from the transaction and mapped into the payment medium at runtime.

FPAYH_OTV

Each party structure carries a consistent set of address component fields (street, house number, building, floor, PO box, room, postal code, city, township, district, region/state, region name, country) plus up to four name fields. Address number references are held separately in FPAYH_SAD.

Which Address Components are Included?

The structured address model includes fields such as:


Address ComponentExample
StreetMain Street
House Number123
BuildingBuilding A
Floor5
Room502
CityShanghai
TownshipPudong
DistrictZhangjiang
Postal Code200120
RegionShanghai
CountryCN

These fields are exposed through dedicated payment structures that can be mapped into payment medium formats. 

The International Address Version: Paying Suppliers in Their Native Script

For multinational organizations that pay suppliers in countries with non-Latin scripts — Chinese characters, Arabic, Cyrillic, Hangul, Kanji, Thai — a single standard address is not enough. SAP's Business Partner master data supports multiple International Address Versions, each assigned a language key (C = Chinese, A = Arabic, G = Greek, H = Hangul, K = Kanji, R = Cyrillic, T = Thai).

The structured address feature integrates directly with this capability. By assigning an Address Version to a payment medium format selection variant, you tell the payment run to fetch the international address of the specified version and populate the structured address fields in the payment file accordingly.

How the Address Version Selection Works

The selection variant is configured in the Create/Assign Selection Variants activity. The following is an example:

  • Selection variant DEBK2 is linked to Address Version C (Chinese).
  • When company code 1010 processes a payment using house bank DEBK2, the system uses this variant.
  • The payment run then fetches the Version C address from the Business Partner master record and writes it into the payment medium file.

If no international address of the requested version exists for a party, the system falls back to the standard (basic) address. 

Configuration & Verification

Structured Address

The following section provides a step-by-step demonstration of how to configure the structured address solution in your system.

Demo scenario: Create a supplier payment where Company Code 1010 acts as the debtor (payer) and Supplier 10300001 acts as the creditor (payee). The purpose of the test is to verify that the structured address maintained for the paying company is correctly populated in the debtor postal address section of the payment medium file.

Step 1 — Create a Format Mapping with Structured Address Fields

Take adding the attributes for the Debtor party as an example. Under the Dbtr node, I created a subnode PstlAdr_New and added the street name, building number, floor, room, and other address attributes.

Open the Map Format Data for Payments app (ID: F2685A).

1. In the Mapping Type filter, select PAYM (Payment Medium Format).

2. Copy Format Mapping from DE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 to /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9.

3. Open the format mapping /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 and start editing.

4. In Format Mapping Properties, click Create Node to add a new PstlAdr_New subnode under the Dbtr node.

5.  In the Attributes section, maintain generic data for each subnode.

In the Source section, select Structure Field as the mapping procedure.

 

Use the value help to search for the structure field FPAYHX-STREETNM_DBT and add it.

6. Repeat for all fields the payment format requires.

7. Save the changes and release the format.

Step 2 — Assign the Format Mapping to a Payment Medium Format

The format mapping drives which structured address fields are written into the XML output of every payment run using that format.

In the Create Payment Medium Formats configuration activity, copy the format from DE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 to /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9, fill the format tree /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9, and save. 

Step 3 — Assign the Payment Medium Format to a Payment Method and Company Code

In the Set Up Payment Methods for Each Country/Region for Payment Transactions configuration activity, assign the /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 payment medium format to the payment method I want to use.

 

In the Set Up Payment Medium Formats per Company Code configuration activity, assign the payment medium format to the paying company code 1010.

 

Step 4 — Maintain Address in Master Data

In the Edit Addresses for Company Codes configuration activity, maintain the address for company code 1010.

Step 5 — Verification: Create a Payment and Generate Payment Files

Once configured and assigned, the payment medium format automatically populates structured address information during payment medium generation.
I now create a payment to supplier 10300001. The expected result should be that the address information for company code 1010 in the payment files is presented in a structured way.
In the payment media result, I can see that /ZDE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 has been used as the payment media format for the payment.

In the payment file, I can see that the address information of paying company code 1010 has been included in a structured way.

Compare this to the unstructured equivalent, where all address content is merged into two opaque AdrLine elements — the structured version gives downstream systems (correspondent banks, compliance screening, SWIFT, local clearing) precise, independently queryable fields.

International Address Version

Unlike the previous scenario, this test verifies the structured address of the supplier (creditor). The payment medium is configured to retrieve the Chinese international address version (Version C) maintained for the supplier business partner.

Step 1 — Assign an Address Version to a Selection Variant

  1. In the Create/Assign Selection Variants configuration activity, create the selection variant  DEBK2 for the payment medium format /DE_CGI_XML_CT_V9 and house bank DEBK2.

By assigning an Address Version to a payment medium format selection variant, the payment medium generation process attempts to retrieve the corresponding international address version for the relevant business partner. If the requested version exists, the structured address fields in the payment file are populated with that address version; otherwise, the system falls back to the standard address.

2. In the Parameter Specifications dialog, set the Address Version field to the desired version code (e.g., C for Chinese).

 

Step 2 — Maintain Business Partner Address Versions

International address versions are commonly maintained and used for business partners such as suppliers and customers.

Activate International Address Version

This time, I want to pay a Chinese supplier 10300002. The master data of the supplier should include an address version in Chinese.

In the Activate International Address Versions - Client-Specific configuration activity, ensure the C (Chinese) version is active.

Maintain International Address Version in Chinese

1. In the Maintain Business Partner app, open the business partner 10300002.
2. Navigate to the Address tab and click Internat. Versions.
3. Select the Chinese address version, and enter the address information in Chinese.

Step 3 — Verification: Create a Payment and Generate Payment Files

When the company code is 1010 & the house bank is DEBK2, the variant DEBK2 is selected.    

When this variant is used for payment medium creation, the supplier's Chinese international address version should be retrieved and populated into the payment medium file. In the payment file generated, the address information is presented in a structured format using the Chinese address version.

 

Summary

The Structured Address solution replaces traditional free-text address lines with dedicated address components. Through configurable format mappings, support for all major payment parties, and integration with business partner international address versions, organizations can generate payment files that are more compliant, more accurate, and better aligned with ISO 20022 requirements.
All the available structures and fields are available in the SAP Help Portal: Maintaining Format Mappings for Structured Addresses | SAP Help Portal
I hope this blog is help for you to understand the structured address solution better. If you have any questions when setting up the structured address solution in your system, welcome to post them here!

entry.title: US-Based Finance Leader Looking for Your Next (or One Final?!) Adventure?
entry.content:
Hiring for Purpose: A Unique Controller Opportunity at Spectrum Designs and a Question for Our Community

Here's a number that should stop any of us in our tracks: studies estimate that between 50% and 85% of adults on the autism spectrum in the United States are unemployed or underemployed, making it a very significant and underreported employment crises in the country. Coupled with the fact that approximately 1 in 31 children (3.2%) and 1 in 45 adults in the United States are on the spectrum, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this is not an issue that is going away. 

For context, the overall U.S. unemployment rate sits around 4%. The gap is staggering and largely invisible.

Spectrum Designs Foundation is one of the organizations doing something about it. Based in Port Washington, New York, Spectrum is a nonprofit social enterprise built around a simple but powerful idea: that individuals on the autism spectrum and with other disabilities are talented, capable, and deserving of real careers. With ~100 employees, the majority neurodiverse, and over $9M in annual revenue, they have proven that inclusive employment and good business are not in conflict. They are one and the same.

A new chapter and a new opportunity

Spectrum Designs is now implementing SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud as the inaugural pilot customer of a new pilot social impact program called SAP Technology for Good. Accenture is implementing the software as part of this pilot engagement. It is a milestone moment for the organization allowing them to scale business operations, but it also means they need to grow their team.

They are currently hiring a Controller to join their leadership team: someone who will own Spectrum's financial operations within their new SAP environment, partnering closely with their CEO and COO to help drive the next phase of their growth.

👉View full job description here: https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=a09ebbe1dfb3161b&from=shareddesktop_copy

This is not your average finance role. It sits at the intersection of finance expertise, nonprofit stewardship, and genuine social impact. The right person will care about both the numbers and the mission behind them. It's a bonus if they have SAP experience.

Two kinds of "right person"

I want to put two profiles out to this community because I think there are two very different people who could be exactly right for this.

The rising leader. Perhaps you are early in your finance career and looking for a role where your work means something beyond the bottom line. A role where you can grow, lead, and look back in ten years knowing you helped build something that mattered. You may also be an individual on the spectrum with incredible expertise, but maybe you have not been given a fair chance at leading a finance organization -- this could be the opportunity for you!

The purposeful closer. Or perhaps you have spent a distinguished career in finance — you have done the implementations, led the teams, earned the credentials. And now you are asking what comes next. What if the last chapter were the best one? What if you took everything you know and put it in service of a mission that deserves it?

Both paths lead to the same place: a seat at the table at one of the most innovative social enterprises in the country, powered by SAP technology in partnership with Accenture. This is an incredible opportunity to prove that with the right technology in place and the right people at the controls, we can truly help the world run better and improve people's lives.

A question for our community

This gives SAP Cloud ERP customers a built-in way to automate payment execution across traditional and digital currency rails, with no separate implementation project, bank testing, or manual file uploads. Because SAP Pay runs natively inside the ERP environment, finance teams can initiate and manage payments without leaving their existing SAP workflow.

Access every payment rail—traditional and digital—through a single connection, with payment automation, reconciliation, and a unified know-your-customer process that:

  • Supports ACH, EFT, wire, check, and stablecoin payments like USD Coin (USDC).
  • Auto-reconciles every payment to its originating purchase order (PO) or invoice.
  • Covers 89 global corridors—no per-country bank setup required.
  • Autonomously initiates and executes payments using AI agents.

SAP Pay powered by Tereina

Reduce payment costs and drive payment automation with embedded, agentic B2B payments across traditional and digital currency rails.


Key features

Multi-rail payment support—your payment, your option

SAP Pay supports fiat and digital currencies and many payment types. This includes real-time payments, alongside USDC stablecoin payments with native integration to Circle, and an intelligent routing to the optimal rail for each transaction across 40+ currencies—all from a single platform.

Natively embedded in SAP S/4HANA

SAP Pay ships as an out-of-the-box capability inside SAP Cloud ERP, with secure bank communication handled via SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity. There’s no implementation project, no new vendor contract, and no custom code—customers activate it inside existing SAP workflow and it runs.

Agentic payment execution

SAP Pay embeds payment execution into SAP now, the foundational step toward agentic payments. The AI agents that already support your finance team through Joule will soon trigger and execute payments, too, closing decision to execution in one flow.

SAP Pay

entry.title: UX improvements in Manage Workflows: Outcome Handling Replaces Exception Handling
entry.content:
Following extensive stakeholder and customer feedback, and informed by user research, an improvement has been made to the Manage Workflows app: the Exception Handling feature has been renamed to Outcome Handling, and field labels have been updated to more accurately reflect the configurations they represent.
 
A big thank you to everyone who contributed — UX, User Assistance, and Development — for the collaboration that made this happen.

 

What Changed

 

The rename touches following things:
 
Before (up to 2608) After (from 2702)
Section name: Exception HandlingSection name: Outcome Handling
Field: Required ActionField: Add Step
Field: Action ResultField: Follow-up Action
Default value: Do nothingDefault value: None

Before:

After:

 

The underlying behavior — what happens when a workflow step ends with a negative outcome such as a rejection — is unchanged. All existing follow-up actions (Cancel Workflow, Continue, Repeat Step, Restart Workflow, Repeat Parallel Steps, Continue with Next Step) remain available (if allowed for a step) with identical semantics.

 

 Why the Rename Makes Sense

 
The old term *Exception Handling* carried a technical connotation, implying something had gone wrong unexpectedly. But a rejection in an approval workflow is not an exception — it's a normal, anticipated outcome. A manager rejecting a purchase request is business as usual; the workflow should handle it gracefully, not treat it as an error.

 

Outcome Handling is more accurate: it describes the deliberate design of what the process should do - in response to any step result - , negative or otherwise. In case of a positive outcome the process continues; negative outcomes require configuration to define how to proceed.

 

The field rename from Required Action → Add Step and Action Result → Follow-up Action follows the same logic. The old labels mixed intent (what the system requires) with result (what the system then does). The new labels describe the configuration in plain process terms: you optionally insert an additional step, and then you choose a follow-up action that determines how the workflow continues.

What This Means for You

 

  • No reconfiguration needed. Existing workflows are unaffected. The behavior you configured under Exception Handling is preserved exactly.
  • Updated documentation. The SAP Help Portal reflects the new terminology from release 2702 onward. Search for *Outcome Handling* when looking up this feature going forward.
  • Onboarding gets easier. New users configuring a workflow step for the first time but also users who do not work with the app on a daily basis will find the section and field names more intuitive, reducing the need to consult documentation just to understand what a field does.

 

Where to Find It

Open the Manage Workflows app, navigate to a workflow step, and scroll to the Outcome Handling section on the Step Details page. Select an optional step to insert in the Add Step field, then choose how the workflow continues in the Follow-up Action dropdown.

 

Available from SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2702.

 

*This post was drafted with the assistance of Claude Code (AI) and checked by SAPs Joule Work desktop. All content has been reviewed and is the responsibility of the author.*

entry.title: S/4HANA to Datasphere: Handling Real-World Data Quality Issues
entry.content:
When moving data from S/4HANA into SAP Datasphere, it is easy to assume that the difficult part is the modeling.

In practice, I found that some of the more time-consuming problems appeared before the modeling logic became the problem at all.

We were working on an analytics project where S/4HANA data was being brought into Datasphere and then exposed for SAP Analytics Cloud reporting. The overall architecture was straightforward: bring the required source data into Datasphere, build the transformation and semantic layers, and consume the resulting models in SAC.

What made the work interesting was what happened when we started looking closely at the data.

A field could exist in S/4HANA, be available in the source view, appear in Datasphere, and still not behave the way we expected once it was used in a model. That changed the way I approached data quality. I stopped treating it as something to check after the model was built. It became part of the modeling process itself.

Data availability does not mean data readiness

One of the first assumptions I had to challenge was: "If the field exists in the S/4HANA source, it should be ready for reporting."

That isn't necessarily true.

A field can be technically available but still create problems for the analytical model. In the project, the issues generally fell into three areas:

Technical issues

  • Data types and invalid values
  • Replication constraints
  • Missing or incomplete source records

Structural issues

  • Joins changing the expected population
  • Unexpected aggregation behaviour
  • Differences between source views and underlying data

Semantic issues

  • GL account mappings
  • Master-data relationships
  • Business classifications that did not align with the transactional population

This becomes particularly important when the data is consumed through several layers.

For example:
S4/HANA → Replication/Ingestion → Local Table → Integration/Harmonization → Reporting Model → SAC

A problem introduced at the source can therefore become visible several layers later. By the time the SAC chart shows an unexpected number, the actual cause may be several transformations away. That was one of the first lessons I took from the project.

The source view is not always the source of truth

One of the issues we encountered involved a CDS-based source that looked suitable for replication.

The view exposed the business fields required for the reporting requirement, so from a functional perspective it looked like the right starting point. The problem appeared when we checked the technical requirements for the Replication Flow.

The CDS view did not provide key fields required for the replication approach we were using. That meant that although the view was useful from a business and semantic perspective, it was not suitable as a direct replication source.

This was one of those issues that is easy to discover late if the focus is only on the fields exposed by the source.

We therefore had to look one layer deeper and identify the underlying data structure that could support the required replication approach.

Instead of asking: "Which CDS view contains the field I need?"
We started asking: "What is the actual persistence and replication requirement behind this field?"

That led us toward the underlying local/raw data structure instead.

This distinction is important because a source object can be perfectly valid from an application or semantic perspective and still not be the right object for a particular data integration pattern.

In other words:
Business-readable source ≠ automatically replication-ready source

That is something I would now check much earlier in a Datasphere implementation.

A field existing in two places does not mean the two fields are equivalent

Another issue appeared when working with GL account information and semantic tagging.

In the project, we were using a semantic-tagging structure containing roughly 1,500 GL account entries to support the financial reporting logic. At the same time, the underlying financial transactional data contained a much larger population of around 20 lakh records.

At first, it was tempting to assume that the semantic-tagging table represented the complete population that should exist in the transactional data.

When we started reconciling the two, that assumption did not hold.

The accounts available in the semantic-tagging structure did not fully correspond to the accounts appearing in the transactional population. We also had to consider the chart of accounts being used in the reporting scope rather than treating every tagged account as universally applicable.

That changed the nature of the investigation.

At that point, the question was no longer: "Why doesn't my join work?"
The better question was: "Are these two datasets actually describing the same business population?"

That distinction matters.

A mapping or semantic table can contain valid business definitions that are broader than the current transactional dataset.

It may contain:

  • accounts not currently used
  • accounts belonging to another scope
  • accounts from another chart of accounts
  • historical values
  • values maintained for future reporting requirements

So seeing an account in a semantic table does not prove that the account should appear in the fact data. The join itself was not necessarily wrong.

Our assumption about the relationship between the datasets was what needed to be investigated.

The zero-value problem that looked like a calculation issue

The most interesting example came from financial measures.

We were working with an amount measure from the financial transaction data. The requirement was to present certain financial values using the reporting sign expected by the business.

We created an inverted amount measure.

The expectation was straightforward: Source amount - invert the sign as a positive reporting value where required. Instead, the resulting measure was showing zero in the analytical output.

Initially, this looked like a calculation problem.

Was the inversion expression wrong?
Was the aggregation wrong?
Was SAC interpreting the measure incorrectly?

But when we went back to the underlying data, the situation became clearer. The issue was not simply the inversion.

The underlying financial data contained positive and negative postings whose aggregation behavior needed to be understood before applying the reporting transformation.

In other words, we were trying to solve a business-sign problem at the measure level before fully understanding the accounting behavior of the underlying records.

That was an important distinction.

A calculated measure can be technically correct and still produce an unexpected business result if the assumptions about the source data are wrong.

Don't debug the final measure first

This experience changed the way I troubleshoot Datasphere models.

When an SAC KPI or chart shows an unexpected value, my first instinct now is not to modify the SAC calculation. I work backwards.

  1. What does the SAC widget actually receive?
    Is the problem already present in the analytical model?
  2. What does the analytical model return?
    If the value is already wrong here, SAC is probably not the root cause.

  3. What does the underlying fact view contain?
    Check the actual records before aggregation.

  4. What did the harmonization layer do?
    Look for joins, filters, calculated columns, and semantic restrictions.

  5. What was actually replicated?
    Finally, go back to the raw/local table and compare it with the source.

The flow becomes:
SAC result → Analytical Model → Fact View → Harmonization View → Local Table → S4/HANA Source

This sounds obvious, but it saves a surprising amount of time. If the value is already incorrect in the fact view, changing the SAC story is unlikely to solve anything.

Data quality is also about semantics

Another lesson was that data quality isn't limited to things such as nulls, invalid dates, or duplicate records. There is another category that is much harder to detect: semantic correctness.

A value can be:

  • populated
  • correctly typed
  • successfully replicated
  • successfully joined

and still be wrong for the business meaning we are trying to represent. The GL account example made this particularly clear. The account value itself could be perfectly valid. The problem was whether it represented the same reporting meaning as the account we were trying to map it to.

The same principle applies to:

  • Company Code
  • Sales Organization
  • Customer
  • Material
  • Currency
  • Fiscal Period
  • Cost Center
  • GL Account

A technically valid join does not automatically mean a semantically valid relationship. 

This is why I increasingly think of data quality in Datasphere in three layers:
Technical quality → Can the data be loaded and queried? → Structural quality → Does the data model relate correctly? → Semantic quality → Does the data mean what the business thinks it means?

All three need to be validated.

When the data looks correct, but the model is wrong

There was another class of issue that initially pointed us toward the source data but eventually turned out to be related to the model.

For example, a source dataset could contain the expected records, but after introducing a join or restriction in a graphical view, the resulting dataset could change significantly. This is where row-level validation becomes useful.

Suppose the raw layer contains:
200,000 records

After a transformation:
198,500 records

That difference is not automatically a problem. But it should be explainable.

Were 1,500 records intentionally filtered?
Did a join remove unmatched records?
Did a condition exclude null values?
Did the semantic mapping only cover part of the population?
Or was the relationship itself incorrect?

A model should not simply produce a number. The change in population between layers should have a reason.

The importance of checking the intermediate layer

One of the practices I found particularly useful was validating intermediate outputs instead of waiting until the final analytical model.

For example:

LayerWhat I should validate
RawRecord availability and source values
HarmonizationJoins, mappings, and transformations
Reporting Measures, aggregation, and business rules
SACFilters, dimensions, and visual output

This gives each layer a responsibility. If something changes between two layers, we know where to investigate. Without that separation, debugging becomes much more difficult because the final result contains the combined effect of everything that happened before it.

Data quality issues are often architecture issues in disguise

One of the broader lessons from this work is that a data problem is not always solved by cleaning the data. Sometimes the problem is where we decided to implement something.

For example:

  • A mapping embedded in a calculation may belong in a reference table.
  • A source field that cannot be reliably replicated may require a different ingestion approach.
  • A business classification may belong in the semantic layer rather than the SAC story.
  • A sign transformation may require a clearer definition of the underlying accounting behavior.
  • A missing relationship may indicate that the master-data model needs to be reconsidered.

This is why I don't see data quality and architecture as completely separate topics. The way we model data affects the way we can detect and explain quality issues.

What I would check earlier next time

After working through these issues, I would add a few checks much earlier in the project.

Validate the source before designing the model

Don't start with the target SAC chart. Start by understanding the source population.

Check replication suitability early

A source view may expose the right business fields but still not satisfy the requirements of the chosen replication mechanism.

Profile critical fields

For fields such as GL Account, Company Code, Currency, and dates, understand the actual values before building dependent logic.

Validate mappings independently

Don't wait for a final reporting number to tell you that two mapping structures don't align. Check the mapping population separately.

Reconcile record counts between layers

Whenever records disappear or multiply, know why.

Validate measures before building the story

A KPI should already be trusted at the model level before it becomes a polished SAC tile. 

These checks don't necessarily require a large additional process. They simply move validation earlier, when fixing a problem is cheaper.

The bigger lesson

Working with S/4HANA data in Datasphere changed my understanding of what "data quality" means in an analytics project.

Initially, I thought of data quality mostly as a source-data problem. After working through the implementation, I see it differently.

There are at least three questions we need to answer:

  • Is the data technically valid?
  • Is it structurally correct for the model?
  • Does it represent the business meaning we think it represents?

The third question is usually the hardest. 
A Datasphere model can activate successfully.
The replication can complete successfully.
The SAC story can display successfully.
And the result can still be wrong.

That is why I now prefer to trace an unexpected number all the way back through the model instead of trying to fix the final output immediately.

The most useful question is often not: "Why is this number wrong?"
It is: "At which layer did this number stop representing what the business intended?"

Once that question becomes part of the development process, troubleshooting becomes less about trial and error and more about understanding how the data moved through the architecture.

For me, that has been one of the more valuable lessons from working with S/4HANA data in SAP Datasphere.

entry.title: Adding New Text Fields: Text Determination Configuration Guide for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
Adding New Text Fields: Text Determination Configuration Guide for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (SD Module)

Scope: Text Determination for SD Documents | Example: Outbound Delivery Header (Text Object VBBK, Procedure T6)

Category: Logistics / Sales and Distribution / Text Determination Configuration

Introduction

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, keeping business processes standardized while staying within the Clean Core principle really matters. A common requirement in the Sales and Distribution module is adding extra text fields, at header or item level, on documents such as Sales Orders, Outbound Deliveries and Billing Documents, so that teams like Sales, Logistics or Finance can record information that the standard text types simply do not cover.

Since traditional SPRO backend access is restricted in the Public Edition, this guide walks through how to add new text fields using SSCUI (Self Service Configuration UI) activities only. As a practical example, we add two new text fields to the Outbound Delivery header, but the same approach works for other documents and levels too. No custom fields, no Adapt UI changes, and no development work are needed for this.

  1. Business Requirement & Scope

For our example, the Logistics and Transport team needed two extra text fields at the Outbound Delivery header level, so that Vehicle Number and Cartage Contractor details could be captured directly on the delivery document, without a separate Z table or a custom field. This information is used purely for reference and tracking as the document moves through the process.

  • Text Object: VBBK (SD Document Header)
  • New Text Types: ZX01 (Vehicle No.) and ZX02 (Cartage Contractor)
  • Text Determination Procedure: T6 (Delivery Header)
  • Applicable documents: Outbound Delivery, for all delivery types that use procedure T6 (used here as the example document)

  1. Configuration Objects Created

The table below lists the objects created and maintained through SSCUI activities in Manage Your Solution to achieve this requirement.

Object Type

Technical ID

Purpose / Description

Text Type

ZX01

Vehicle No., new text type used to capture the vehicle number on the delivery header

Text Type

ZX02

Cartage Contractor, new text type used to capture the contractor details on the delivery header

Access Sequence

9000

Access sequence linked to the Vehicle No. text ID

Access Sequence

9001

Access sequence linked to the Cartage Contractor text ID

Text Determination Procedure

T6

Delivery Header procedure, both new text IDs assigned here at sequence 20 and 25

 

  1. Step-by-Step Configuration

Step 1: Define New Text Types (SSCUI 105684)

Go to Manage Your Solution and search for 105684. Open the activity Define Text Types for SD Document Header. This activity works on text object VBBK, which covers the SD document header.

SSCUI search result for activity 105684, Define Text Types for SD Document Header

SSCUI search result for activity 105684, Define Text Types for SD Document Header

Add two new entries here, ZX01 for Vehicle No. and ZX02 for Cartage Contractor.

New text type entries ZX01 (Vehicle No.) and ZX02 (Cartage Contractor) added under text object VBBK

Step 2: Set Up Text Determination for the Delivery Header (SSCUI 101291)

Next, go back to Manage Your Solution and search for 101291, Set Up Text Determination for Delivery Header.

SSCUI search result for activity 101291, Set Up Text Determination for Delivery Header

Inside this activity, select procedure T6, Delivery Header, and then click Text IDs in Procedure in the dialog structure on the left.

Text Determination Procedures screen, T6 Delivery Header selected

Step 3: Assign the New Text IDs to Procedure T6

Enter the new text ID entries under T6. ZX01 is placed at sequence 20 and ZX02 at sequence 25, both set as Text Is Not Mandatory, and linked to access sequences 9000 and 9001 respectively.

Text IDs in Procedure T6, entries ZX01 and ZX02 added

Step 4: Create the Access Sequences

From the same dialog structure, click Access Sequences and add the new entries, 9000 for Vehicle No. and 9001 for Cartage Contractor.

Access Sequences list, 9000 and 9001 created for the new text IDs

Step 5: Maintain Access Sequence for Text IDs

Click Access Sequence for Text IDs and, for sequence 9000, add an entry pointing to text object VBBK (Sales: Header texts), ID ZX01, with All Languages checked. Repeat the same for sequence 9001, this time pointing to ID ZX02.

Access Sequence 9000 detail, mapped to text ID ZX01 (Vehicle No.)

Access Sequence 9001 detail, mapped to text ID ZX02 (Cartage Contractor)

Save the configuration once both access sequences are maintained.

  1. Verification on the Outbound Delivery

Once both SSCUI activities are saved, the new fields are ready to use. Here is how to check them:

  1. Open or create an Outbound Delivery, using the Create Outbound Delivery or Change Outbound Delivery app.
  2. Go to Header Details and select the Texts tab.
  3. The two new text types, Vehicle No. and Cartage Contractor, now appear in the list along with the standard text types.
  4. Select either one and enter free text, exactly like any other header text.

Outbound Delivery header, Texts tab, before the configuration

Outbound Delivery header, Texts tab, after the configuration, Vehicle No. and Cartage Contractor now available

  1. Adding More Text Fields or Using the Same Approach for Other Documents

Everything above was done for the Outbound Delivery header, but nothing in the approach is specific to it. Text determination works the same way across SD documents, so you can repeat it whenever a new text field is needed. Here are the most common cases:

  • More fields on the same document: repeat Steps 1 to 5 with a new text ID (for example ZX03), a new sequence number in procedure T6 and a new access sequence.
  • Other header texts, such as Sales Order or Billing Document: use the text determination activity for that document and select the matching value in the Group for field on the Text Determination Procedures screen. The rest of the flow stays the same.
  • Item level texts: work with the item text object and the item text determination procedure instead, then follow the same pattern of text type, procedure entry, access sequence and mapping.
  • Assigning the procedure to the right document types: use the Text Procedure Assignment node in the dialog structure, so that the document types you want actually pick up the procedure.

A few practical tips: keep new text IDs and access sequences in the customer namespace (for example Z prefixed text IDs and 9000 and 9001 for access sequences as used here), decide upfront whether a text should be mandatory using the Text Is Mandatory setting, and always confirm the result in the app before moving the configuration further. The exact SSCUI activity names can differ by document, so search for them in Manage Your Solution using the document name.

Conclusion

In this guide we created two new header text types (ZX01 Vehicle No. and ZX02 Cartage Contractor) under text object VBBK, assigned them to the Delivery Header procedure T6 with their own access sequences (9000 and 9001), and confirmed on the Outbound Delivery that both fields now appear in the Texts tab and accept free text. All of this was done with standard SSCUI activities only, so the Clean Core approach stays intact. If a new text does not show up on your document, check that the text ID is saved in the procedure, that the access sequence points to the correct text object and ID, and that the procedure is assigned to the document type you are testing. The same pattern can be repeated for more fields or for other SD documents.

Activation and Authorization of AI-assisted Analytical Business Insights

 

Activation

To activate this AI-assisted feature, submit an incident on component BC-CTS-EXM-CNT. For more information on the activation process, see the Knowledge Base Article 3651017 - Activation of SAP Business AI Features in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - SAP for Me.

Authorization

Assign the business catalog SAP_BW_BC_RVB_ABI_PC to a role. When you create a new role in the Maintain Business Roles app, the write access defaults to No Access. Change the Write, Read, Value Help access category from No Access to Unrestricted or Restricted. If you select Restricted, update the restrictions based on your requirements.
